opus-5.5.text:
I think the first principle is that an architecture has to be hardware-friendly. That sounds obvious, but it's often underestimated. In a scaling-oriented world, what matters isn't just how expressive a model is in theory. It's how much useful computation you can get out of a GPU per dollar and per second. A lot of ideas that look elegant on paper, like certain recurrent formulations or fancy state-space updates, end up losing because they can't use tensor cores efficiently, or because they're memory-bound. The Transformer won partly because attention is basically big matrix multiplications, and that maps beautifully onto modern hardware. So when I work on efficient architectures like linear attention or DeltaNet, a big part of the work is reformulating the computation, for example into chunkwise parallel forms, so it actually runs fast in practice and not just with better asymptotic complexity.

The second principle is that the architecture should scale gracefully. That means not only with parameters and data, but also with context length and with inference demands. Today inference cost matters as much as training cost, especially with reasoning models generating very long chains of thought. Softmax attention has a KV cache that grows linearly with sequence length, which becomes a real bottleneck. So there's a strong motivation for architectures with a constant-size or more compressed state. But you have to do that without sacrificing too much quality, especially on things like in-context retrieval, where pure linear models have historically been weaker.

The third principle is to be principled about what the model's memory is actually doing. One way I like to think about it is that a recurrent state is like a fast-weight memory, and the update rule is essentially an online learning algorithm. Vanilla linear attention just keeps adding key-value outer products, which is a pretty crude way to write to memory. The delta rule instead says: correct the memory based on the prediction error. Gating adds a way to forget. Viewing it this way gives you a design space grounded in optimization, rather than ad hoc tricks, and it tends to lead to things that both work better and are easier to reason about.

Finally, I'd say we should be pragmatic rather than ideological. I don't think the answer is "Transformers versus RNNs." Hybrid architectures, mixing a few full-attention layers with many efficient linear or recurrent layers, are already showing a very good trade-off, and several industry models have adopted that. Ultimately, the bitter lesson still applies: the designs that win are the ones that let you throw more compute and data at the problem most effectively. Our job as architecture researchers is to remove the bottlenecks that stop that from happening.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the first principle is that an architecture has to respect the hardware. That sounds obvious, but a lot of elegant ideas die because they don't map well onto GPUs. The question I always ask is whether the core operation can be expressed as large matrix multiplications that saturate the tensor cores, and whether memory movement is small relative to compute. If the answer is no, the idea has to be dramatically better in quality to justify itself, and usually it isn't.

The second principle is to pay attention to training parallelism, not just inference. Linear attention and state space models are attractive because inference is constant memory per token, but if the recurrence can only be run sequentially, you lose the whole reason transformers won. A lot of my own work on things like gated linear attention has really been about finding formulations where the recurrence has a chunkwise parallel form, so you train with matmuls and you decode with a small state. Both sides have to work.

Third, I'd say you need to think in terms of scaling curves rather than single data points. Many architectures look great at a few hundred million parameters and then the gap to attention closes or reverses. You have to be honest about that and run matched compute comparisons across a range of sizes before claiming anything.

And then there's a more philosophical point, which is that the recurrent state is really a form of memory, and the design question is how the model reads from and writes to that memory. Once you frame it that way, a lot of recent models look like different update rules on the same object. Something like DeltaNet is essentially doing an online gradient step on an associative memory. I find that lens useful because it tells you what expressivity you're buying with each change, instead of just stacking gates until the loss goes down.

Finally, I think hybrids are the pragmatic answer right now. A few layers of full attention mixed with linear layers recovers most of the retrieval ability that pure linear models struggle with, while keeping most of the efficiency. Purity is nice for a paper, but the systems that actually get deployed tend to be whatever combination gives the best quality per unit of hardware cost.

astra-6.text:
I think the first principle is to design for the scale you actually care about. An architecture that looks good in a small experiment may not be the best choice when you increase the model size, the amount of data, or the context length. So we should look at how its performance improves with more resources, rather than just comparing results at one scale.

The second principle is to treat efficiency as part of the architecture itself. FLOPs are useful, but they don’t tell you everything. Memory access, communication, and how well the operations run on the hardware all affect how much you can train within a fixed budget. A theoretically efficient design isn’t necessarily efficient in practice.

And finally, I would favor simplicity and stability. Every additional mechanism should justify its complexity through a consistent benefit. The goal is to build something that learns effectively, scales predictably, and remains practical to train and use.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the first principle is to design for how the model scales, rather than just how it performs at one particular size. An architectural change that helps a small model may not remain useful when you increase parameters, data, or training compute. So you want to study the scaling behavior, not just compare a few benchmark numbers.

The second principle is to measure efficiency in the actual system. FLOPs are useful, but memory access, communication, hardware utilization, and training stability all affect what you can accomplish with a fixed budget. A theoretically efficient architecture can still be slow to train.

And third, I would favor simplicity unless added complexity produces a clear, repeatable benefit. The architecture should have a strong reason for each component. Ultimately, the question is: does this design let us turn more compute and more data into better capabilities, reliably and efficiently?
